title: Humbler Than a Blade of Grass
hookLine: a grammar teacher comes home from pilgrimage and every word he explains turns into Krishna
carry: kirtan: the name, sung humbler than grass
last: A CHILD MAY BRING HER ANYTHING.

cards: What happens to a grammar lesson when the teacher can only think of God?
In Nabadwip, a town of scholars on the river, the teacher is young and sharp, known for his skill in Sanskrit grammar, and his students are proud to study with him.
Then he goes away on a pilgrimage, and comes back different. He sits down to explain an ordinary word, a verb, a root, and somehow the explanation ends in Krishna. The next word, the same.
The students look at each other. They came for grammar. Today, the Vaishnava stream, and a teacher you met earlier on this path: Chaitanya.

teach.b: The biographies tell this story, and they don't make fun of the students. In the end he closes the school. He can't teach grammar anymore, because every word has become a door to the same room.
So what does he do instead? He sings.
With friends, in a courtyard at first, then out in the streets of Nabadwip: the names of God, Hari, Krishna, over and over to drums and cymbals, louder and faster, until people are dancing.
That's kirtan, and in this stream it isn't decoration.

teach.h: THE NAME, SUNG IN THE STREETS
teach.b: It is the practice: the name, sung out loud, in company. The singing could sound like showing off.

teach.h: HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS
teach.b: But Chaitanya is remembered for a handful of short teaching verses, and one of them, in paraphrase, says how to sing: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor to others and wanting none for yourself.
A tree, the old explanation goes, gives shade even to the one who cuts it down. So the loudest practice in the stream is meant to come from the lowest place.
Remember the conch on Bengal's first day, the Goddess as Mother? The Vaishnava stream also reaches for a close name.
For Chaitanya's followers the closest of all is Radha's love for Krishna, and in their stories Chaitanya himself weeps and longs for Krishna the way Radha does.
The scholar who couldn't stop saying Krishna ends up singing in the street, as low as grass.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who follow Chaitanya, gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to the khol drum and hand cymbals, and some take the singing into the streets.

games.q: what does “bengal's shakta and vaishnava streams” mean?
o: Bengal's schools of Sanskrit grammar along the river
Bengal's ways of loving God as Mother and as Krishna
a set of rules for keeping devotion quiet and private

games.q: Chaitanya in Nabadwip — tap the pairs.
p: the names of God sung together

s: Chaitanya kept his devotion quiet and private
he sang the names of God out loud, with others, in the streets.
one of his verses says to sing humbler than a blade of grass
and more patient than a tree, honoring others and wanting no honor.
in this stream, kirtan is just decoration around the real practice
the name, sung in company, is the practice.

games.q: you're Chaitanya. you come back from pilgrimage, and every word you try to teach turns into Krishna. what do you do?
o: force yourself back to plain grammar.
close the school and sing the names in the streets.
write a grammar book about Krishna.
games.why: the biographies say he closed the school, and the singing that followed spilled out into the streets of Nabadwip.

practice: On the in-breath, picture a blade of grass, low, bending when it's walked on, standing up again; on the out-breath, a tree, rooted, patient, giving shade.
Go back and forth, grass and tree, and bring to mind one person who might need you to bend, or to wait. If you pray, let a name of God, Hari or Krishna or your own, sound softly with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: the Vaishnava stream in Chaitanya, the grammar teacher who sang the names of Krishna in the street, humbler than a blade of grass. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: kirtan, the name sung humbler than grass. Every word, a door to the same room. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Bhagavata (Vrindavan Das) and Chaitanya Charitamrita (Krishnadasa Kaviraja): the return from Gaya, the closing of the school, kirtan in Nabadwip
